attempts.report: Diagnosis: Frost. The flower shows a dark, irregularly shaped blotch on the receptacle, the anthers are brown and shriveled, the petals are slightly wilted, and the surrounding green sepals are slightly curled, all indicating cold injury rather than disease. The discoloration is concentrated on the exposed, sun-exposed receptacle, and the damage is patchy rather than uniform across the blossom, consistent with a brief, localized freeze event. The surrounding foliage remains green and intact, suggesting the injury was limited to the exposed flower head rather than spreading systemically. These clues point to overnight temperatures dropping below 0 °C (32 °F) that scorched the developing fruit. To protect future blooms, install a floating row cover or lightweight fleece over the bed each evening when forecasts predict temperatures below 2 °C (36 °F), and add a 5 cm (2 in) layer of clean straw mulch to buffer soil temperature and trap moisture. Irrigate the root zone to a depth of 5 cm (2 in) before the next predicted freeze, and clear any debris or weeds that could limit airflow and trap cold air. Over the next seven days, visually check each morning for new blackened centers on developing berries, note any additional wilting or yellowing of leaves, and confirm that row covers remain in place until daybreak; also press a finger 5 cm (2 in) into the soil to confirm it stays moist but not waterlogged.

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Root rot. The majority of the root system appears dark brown-black and stringy rather than creamy white, several fine feeder roots are missing or shriveled, the remaining roots are thin and brittle rather than firm and fibrous, and the crown area shows a soft, water-soaked surface with slight collapse. These clues point to prolonged saturation that favored soil-borne fungi and bacteria that suffocate the root cortex. Immediately lift the plant into a raised bed or mound 15–20 cm high and amend the top 15 cm with 5 cm of coarse composted bark to improve drainage; thereafter irrigate only when the upper 3 cm of soil is dry, applying about 2 cm of water in the early morning so the root zone dries quickly. Remove and discard the visibly rotted roots with sterile shears and space remaining plants 30 cm apart to improve airflow. Over the next week, check daily for any new blackening or softening of roots, probe soil moisture at 5 cm depth with a finger to ensure it feels barely damp but not wet, and watch for emergence of fresh white feeder roots—absence of new white growth or continued crown collapse signals the need for further drainage adjustments.

The crown and primary roots of the plant show a dark, water-soaked, almost blackened appearance, with a brittle, shriveled texture; fine feeder roots are sparse and absent, leaving a prominent, darkened central core; the root system appears compacted and lacking the normal fibrous, branching pattern; and the overall tissue appears mushy and decayed, suggesting extensive rot. These visual cues point to prolonged saturation and poor aeration that favored soil-borne fungi and bacteria. Immediately improve drainage by raising the bed 15–20 cm and blending in 30 % coarse compost or perlite to break up the heavy clay; irrigate only when the top 5 cm of soil is dry, applying about 2.5 cm of water in the early morning so foliage dries quickly; and remove and discard the affected plant, sanitizing tools with 10 % bleach solution for 1 minute before reusing. Over the next 7 days, check daily for any new darkening or slimy texture at the crown base, probe soil moisture at 5 cm depth to ensure it stays moist but not wet, and observe emerging root tips for fresh white growth instead of further browning.

The crown and lower 20 cm of the root system are dark brown to black, water-soaked and collapsing, fine feeder roots are sparse or missing, and the cortex shows a uniform darkening rather than the normal creamy white color. These visual cues point to a fungal or oomycete infection that thrives in saturated, poorly aerated soil.
Recommendations: (1) immediately stop overhead irrigation and switch to drip or furrow watering, delivering 2–3 cm (≈1 in) of water every 4–5 days, allowing the top 5 cm of soil to dry between waterings; (2) raise the planting bed or mound 15–20 cm high and incorporate 30 % coarse compost or perlite to improve drainage; (3) remove and discard all visibly rotted roots and crown tissue, sanitizing tools with 70 % alcohol between cuts; (4) apply a 2 cm layer of clean straw mulch to reduce splash and keep the root zone cooler, but keep mulch 5 cm away from the crown; (5) space plants at least 30 cm apart to boost airflow and reduce humidity around neighboring crowns. Over the next 7 days, check daily for any new blackening or slimy roots, probe soil moisture to 5 cm depth to ensure it is only slightly moist, and note any fresh white root tips emerging from the crown as an early sign of recovery.

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Overwatered. The soil surface appears uniformly dark, glossy, and compacted, indicating saturation; the potting mix is not breathing and lacks the light-brown, crumbly texture expected after a thorough drying. The crown and lower stem are pale, slightly translucent, and slightly sunken, showing early root suffocation, while the single remaining leaf is limp and curled downward, both classic signs of oxygen starvation. The fruit truss hangs limp and lacks the bright red color normally seen on ripening berries, suggesting stagnant nutrient flow. No visible white root tips or white, fuzzy growth on the crown are present, further confirming excess moisture rather than nutrient deficiency. Together these clues point to overwatering that has limited oxygen and slowed root activity. Allow the top 2.5 cm (1 in) of soil to dry before the next irrigation, then water only until water drains from the bottom drainage holes; elevate the pot on 2 cm (¾ in) spacers to improve airflow under the canopy; and gently loosen the upper 2 cm of soil with a fork to break up the compacted crust and improve drainage. Over the next week, visually check each morning for the top 2 cm of soil feeling dry to the touch, watch for the appearance of firm, upright new leaves, and inspect the crown for any regrowth or lightening of color as confirmation of recovery.

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Frost. The leaves are uniformly coated with a dense, dark brown to black necrotic pattern, with individual lesions ranging from 1–5 cm long; many lesions are concentric and sunken, and the margins of affected tissue appear slightly lighter than the rest, indicating tissue death rather than simple spotting. Frost-burned areas are dry and papery, and the overall texture of the foliage is dull rather than glossy, all consistent with cold injury. The surrounding soil appears moist and shaded, and the light-colored mulch looks damp, suggesting overnight watering that left the crown exposed to cold air. These clues point to a recent Frost event that froze and killed interior cells, leaving behind the characteristic necrotic pattern. Immediately stop irrigation for 3 days, then resume only when the top 2.5 cm (1 in) of soil is dry; during the next Frost warning, drape a breathable row cover or fleece over the bed to protect the crown from sub-zero temperatures; and, if night temperatures are forecast below 2 °C (35 °F), apply a 3 cm (1.2 in) layer of clean straw mulch to buffer the crown from radiant heat loss. Over the next week, check each morning for new lesions that spread beyond 5 mm (0.2 in) in diameter, confirm that soil at 5 cm depth dries to the touch within 24 h of watering, and note whether the row cover or mulch remains dry to the touch after sunrise, adjusting protection accordingly.

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Root rot. The root cross-section shows a uniform dark-brown to almost black coloration, with a water-soaked, slightly translucent margin, and a lack of Healthy white feeder roots; the cortex tissue appears stringy and shriveled rather than firm; the outer surface is slightly sunken and lacks the normal fibrous texture; and the entire section is coated with a fine, powdery film that is typical of decay. These visual cues point to extensive root rot caused by prolonged saturation and poor drainage that favors soil-borne pathogens. Immediately improve drainage by raising the bed 15–20 cm and incorporating 30 % coarse compost or perlite into the top 20 cm of soil; irrigate only when the top 5 cm of soil is dry, applying no more than 2.5 cm of water in a single session and allowing the soil to dry before the next watering. Remove and discard the affected plant, and sanitize tools with 10 % bleach solution for 1 minute before replanting. Over the next 7 days, visually check that new roots emerge from the crown area as white and firm, confirm that the soil surface dries to a crusty texture within 24 h after watering, and inspect the crown for any fresh softening or darkening that would signal continuing rot.

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Frost Injury. The plant shows a patchy, irregular pattern of light-green and dark-brown tissue on the upper leaf surface, with several small necrotic lesions concentrated near the midrib, and a slightly shriveled margin that is darker than the rest of the leaf. The discoloration is localized and not uniform across the leaf, and the margins of the affected areas are sharply demarcated from the otherwise healthy tissue, all consistent with cold injury rather than disease. Frost events can rupture cell walls and cause localized freezing that kills cells, resulting in the characteristic patchy, sunken appearance. Temperatures below 2 °C (32 °F) can also trigger rapid water loss and subsequent necrosis, especially when foliage is exposed to wind or poor airflow. To protect the plant, avoid overnight temperatures below 1 °C (34 °F) by providing 30–40 cm (12–16 in) of row cover or moving pots into a cold frame, and ensure soil stays consistently moist but not waterlogged by supplying about 2.5 cm (1 in) of water per week. If nights are forecast to dip below 0 °C (32 °F), apply a 2 cm (¾ in) layer of mulch or straw around the crown to buffer soil temperature and reduce radiant chill. Over the next seven days, inspect the underside of each leaf at dawn for new blackened areas, check soil moisture with a finger test to ensure it stays evenly moist but not soggy, and note any further leaf collapse or edge browning to confirm whether additional cold stress is occurring.

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Gray mold. The berries show a dense, velvety gray-brown fuzz on the calyx ends, softened, water-soaked tissue beneath, and slight shriveling of the fruit surface, while adjacent berries remain firm and red, indicating a localized infection. The fuzz is concentrated where the fruit touches the plastic mulch and the calyxes are trapped in a small, humid pocket, suggesting prolonged surface moisture and poor airflow. These clues point to Botrytis cinerea thriving under high humidity and stagnant air around ripening fruit. Immediately clip and discard all infected berries and any touching debris, then thin foliage so that at least 10 cm (4 in) of open space surrounds each crown; irrigate at soil level early morning with 2 cm (¾ in) water once every 3–4 days, keeping leaves and fruit dry; and lay a clean straw or plastic mulch layer 3 cm (1¼ in) thick beneath clusters to lift fruit off damp soil. Over the next seven days, inspect daily for new gray fuzz on calyxes, check that leaf surfaces dry within two hours after watering, and confirm that the top 2 cm (¾ in) of soil stays moist but not saturated by inserting a finger or moisture probe.

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Frost. The fruit surface shows irregular dark-brown to black patches, some with a slightly sunken, water-soaked look, while adjacent berries remain pale red; several calyxes are collapsed and blackened, and several fruits display uneven ripening with soft, water-soaked areas alongside hard, unblemished ones. The damage is concentrated on the upper half of each berry, and the discoloration is most pronounced on the sun-exposed side, indicating cold injury rather than disease. These clues point to overnight temperatures dipping below 0 °C (32 °F) that froze the fruit tissue, causing localized cell collapse and discoloration. Immediately cover plants with a breathable row cover or straw blanket each evening when forecasts predict temperatures below 2 °C (36 °F), and irrigate to a depth of 10 cm (4 in) before sunset to warm the soil and buffer air temperature. Remove and discard all visibly damaged fruit to reduce inoculum, and thin crowded leaves to improve airflow and reduce future Frost stress. Over the next seven days, check each morning for new blackened areas on fruit shoulders, confirm that soil at 5 cm (2 in) depth remains moist but not waterlogged, and note any additional leaf or flower wilting as an early warning of future Frost events.

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Root rot. The crown and several lower roots are dark brown-black and stringy, the soil surface appears light and powdery, and the exposed crown tissue is soft and water-soaked, while nearby foliage is pale green and wilted. These clues point to excess moisture and oxygen deprivation that have allowed rot-causing fungi to colonize the root zone. Immediately lift the plant onto a 10 cm (4 in) high raised bed or pot with a well-drained mix, and cut out all black, mushy roots while leaving the crown and any white, firm roots intact; then replant with a 3 cm (1¼ in) layer of coarse straw mulch to keep the crown dry. Irrigate only when the top 3 cm (1¼ in) of soil is dry, applying no more than 2 cm (¾ in) of water in a single session, and ensure at least 15 cm (6 in) of airflow between plants by thinning foliage. Over the next seven days, check daily for any fresh blackening at the crown base, probe soil moisture to 5 cm depth to confirm it stays slightly dry, and look for new white root tips emerging from the crown area as evidence of recovery.

attempts.report:
Diagnosis: Root Rot. The crown and fine feeder roots are uniformly dark brown to black, water-soaked, and collapsed, with a slimy texture; many roots appear brittle and shriveled, and there is a faint greyish-white fungal film on the surface; the root mass is confined to a small, shallow pot, and the soil around the crown is saturated and compacted, suggesting prolonged moisture and poor aeration. These visual cues point to root rot caused by water-mold pathogens thriving in stagnant, wet conditions.
Provide immediate care: (1) lift the plant onto a 3–4 cm (1.5 in) high raised bed or bench to improve drainage and airflow, (2) irrigate only when the top 2.5 cm (1 in) of soil is dry, applying no more than 2.5 cm (1 in) of water in a single deep soak, and (3) gently trim away the blackened, mushy roots with sterilized scissors and discard them outside the garden to reduce inoculum. Add a 2 cm (¾ in) layer of coarse bark mulch to keep the crown dry and improve surface aeration, and space the plant at least 25 cm (10 in) from neighbors to boost airflow. Over the next seven days, check daily for any fresh blackening or sour odor at the crown base, probe soil moisture to 2.5 cm depth with a finger to confirm it is just moist, and inspect the crown for firmness and absence of further softening. If any of these checks fail, repeat trimming and adjust irrigation frequency accordingly.

attempts.report: Diagnosis: White mold. The berries show dense, cotton-like white mycelial growth, especially on the lower half of several fruits, while adjacent berries are water-soaked and collapsing; the calyxes are browned and shriveled; several fruits are clustered tightly, trapping moisture; and the infection is most prominent where fruit touches the plastic mulch surface. These visual cues point to Botrytis cinerea thriving under prolonged surface moisture and stagnant air. Immediately clip and discard all visibly infected berries, then thin foliage so that crowns are at least 20 cm (8 in) apart to improve airflow; switch to early-morning drip irrigation delivering about 2 cm (¾ in) of water per week, keeping leaves and fruit dry; and lay a 3 cm (1¼ in) layer of clean straw mulch under the canopy to keep fruit off damp soil. Over the next seven days, visually check daily for any new white tufts on the underside of leaves, note whether berries stay dry within two hours after watering, and verify that no new soft, water-soaked spots appear on the calyxes or fruit shoulders.

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Frost. The leaves display a uniform pale-green to light-yellow cast with a dull, matte sheen, many leaflets are slightly curled and wilted, and the margins show a faint crispness that is more pronounced on the lower, exposed leaves. These visual cues indicate recent exposure to sub-zero temperatures that froze cell sap, causing tissue desiccation and loss of chlorophyll. Frost likely penetrated the canopy when air temperatures dropped below 2 °C (35 °F) and moisture in the foliage froze, causing cellular damage. Provide protection by draping a breathable row cover or fleece over the bed every evening when forecasts predict lows below 2 °C, and ensure the fabric is securely anchored to the ground to prevent wind lifting. Add a 5–7 cm (2–3 in) layer of clean straw mulch around the crowns to trap soil heat and buffer cold air, and water the root zone to a depth of 10 cm (4 in) before the next predicted frost to improve insulation. Over the next week, visually check each morning for new leaf tips turning black or brown, inspect the underside of foliage for additional ice crystals or water-soaked lesions, and use a thermometer to confirm that soil temperatures at 5 cm remain above 4 °C (39 °F) during daylight hours.

These visual cues indicate that the plant has been exposed to sub-zero temperatures that froze and damaged cell walls, resulting in chlorosis and reduced turgor. Immediately cover the bed with a breathable mulch (e.g., straw or leaf litter) or a 3–4 cm layer of soil to buffer the next cold event, and if night temperatures are forecast to drop below 2 °C (36 °F), install a floating row cover or lightweight fleece blanket to trap radiant heat. Irrigate the soil to a depth of 5 cm (2 in) before the next cold spell to release stored moisture and improve insulation, and consider adding a low-emission heating mat or black plastic mulch around the crown to raise soil temperature by 2–3 °C (4 °F). Over the next week, check each morning for new leaf spots or further wilting, probe soil moisture at 5 cm depth to ensure it remains evenly moist but not waterlogged, and note any recovery of leaf color or regained turgor as evidence that the intervention is working.
